newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rwandan Hutus make last stand in Zaire outpost.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan Hutus make last stand in Zaire outpost.

text.p: The 40 or so gendarmes and local officials stationed at the Zairean jungle outpost of Punia have long since gone, leaving the town under the armed occupation of Hutu soldiers of the former Rwandan army.
Lost in a vast expanse of thick jungle canopy, the tin mining town could easily be forgotten in the larger picture of conflict and humanitarian disaster overwhelming eastern Zaire.

But Punia too is receiving its fair share of tragedy in the spreading war between the Zairean army, allied Rwandan Hutu troops and Tutsi-led rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL).

Half the estimated 100,000 civilian population of the town and its surroundings have fled harassment by the ex-FAR. The FAR, or Rwandan Armed Forces troops, led the 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis in Rwanda and then fled to Zaire.
About half a million Hutu refugees that the ex-soldiers used as human shields streamed back to Rwanda late last year as ethnic Tutsis gained the upperhand in fighting in eastern Zaire.
The armed elements in Punia had melted further into the rain forests with hundreds of other civilian Hutu refugees.
"The problem is with the ex-FAR and not the refugees," said local teacher Amuru Kasele. "The ex-FAR have driven the people into the forest by stealing from them and threatening them."
Punia, like dozens of towns before it, is trapped between the notoriously undisciplined and retreating Zairean army, ex-FAR troops, starving Hutu refugees and advancing rebels.
It's a cocktail of woe that the population, who survive largely on subsistence slash-and-burn farming and spinoffs from the local tin mining industry, could do without.
Like the inhabitants of dozens of towns and villages in the region, most of the remaining Zaireans seem persuaded the arrival of the rebel administration is the answer to their woes.

"The best thing that could happen is that the Hutu soldiers leave. The population could then return from the bush. When the others (the rebels) come, there may be peace," said one of the two remaining Zairean officials in the town. They have not received a salary from the central state for over two years.
"We will be very happy when the rebels arrive, because it's time for a change," says teacher Kasele, who has also been without a state salary for years.
Some 180 km (110 miles) to the south in the provincial capital Kindu, rebels have just appointed a new governor for the region after capturing the town last weekend.
To the north, the rebels are approaching Kisangani, the provincial capital of neibouring Upper Zaire Province, sending tens of thousands of bedraggled Hutu refugees fleeing.
Punia, should the rebels arrive and the ex-FAR troops withdraw as the the local population expects, would slip easily into the rapidly expanding territory under AFDL control.
But while locals support such a prospect the 4,000 remaining Rwandan refugees there do not.

"We are planning to leave tommorrow. The rebels have been killing refugees. When I was at Nyasa they fired directly on us, so here too there is a danger they will kill us," said Eric Semasaka, a 27-year-old man whose age and gender make him prime target of the rebels.

Some of the refugees have only just emerged from months in the forest. Now they are preparing to continue their interminable journey away from Rwanda and the retribution they fear for the part they are accused of playing in the genocide.

Rebels have seized a stretch of the east 1,000 km (600 miles) long since October. Efforts by foreign mercenaries to bolster the ramshackle army of President Mobutu Sese Seko have failed because of poor logistics, training and low morale.
